newsitem.title: USA: U.S. experts see no threat Ecuador will default.
newsitem.headline: U.S. experts see no threat Ecuador will default.

text.p: Despite the current political crisis in Ecuador, the country is expected to meet its Brady interest payments on roughly $87 million due on February 28, emerging market debt strategists said.

"I don't see a major problem for the coupon payments. Ecuador has about $1.9 billion in reserves, so from an ability to pay point of view, I don't see a problem," said Tulio Vera, managing director at Bear Stearns & Co Inc.

The payments due in February consist of $39.2 million in Ecuador's PDI bonds and $47.7 million in the country's discount bonds. A $32.3 million payment on the country's par bonds is due May 28, sources said.
Although Ecuadoran Brady bonds have tumbled in recent days, sources said the likelihood of a default was nil.
"It's really not something that people are at all concerned about. We are not at that level of crisis," said Ingrid Iverson, emerging market debt strategist at UBS Securities in New York.
Dan Peirce, emerging market debt strategist at BankBoston Corp, said the financials remain pretty solid at this time.

"The reason we have to be concerned is if there is really a change in the political landscape that would ultimately destroy the solvency issue and it doesn't seem like that is the case at this point, and that is why we have investors looking to buy paper at lower prices," he added.
Over the last two days, Ecuador's PDIs have fallen 3-3/8 to current levels of 58-5/8 bid and its discounts have dropped 2-3/4 to 67-1/2 bid.

Joyce Chang, manager and emerging market debt strategist at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc, said: "We still have it (Ecuador's Bradys) at market weight, at neutral, which we have had it at for months and months. We are keeping it there because we feel comfortable that the debt servicing prospects are fine."
Still, Chang said Merrill would underweight Ecuador's Brady bonds in a more bearish market because upcoming developments are expected to take on a negative tone.

"But because we are not concerned about the debt servicing process and because we feel that the tone in the market is still overall quite strong, we don't see the cause to actually move it right now, but we don't see it as a clear buying opportunity either," she added.
